{{short description|French mathematician}}
'''Victor Gustave Robin''' ({{IPA|fr|viktɔʁ ɡystav ʁɔbɛ̃|lang}}; 17 May 1855 – 1897) was a French [[mathematical]] analyst and [[applied mathematician]] who lectured in mathematical physics at the [[University of Paris|Sorbonne]] in [[Paris]] and also worked in the area of [[thermodynamics]].<ref name=MI>[[Karl Edwin Gustafson|Gustafson, Karl]], and Abe, Takehisa. (Victor) Gustave Robin: 1855–1897, The Mathematical Intelligencer 20 (2) (1998), 47–53.</ref><ref name =MD>Robert C. James, Glenn James, Mathematics Dictionary, Kluwer Academic Publishers 1995, {{ISBN|0-412-99041-5}} p363</ref><ref>[[Karl Edwin Gustafson|Gustafson, K.]], (1998). Domain Decomposition, Operator Trigonometry, Robin Condition, ''Contemporary Mathematics'', '''218'''. 432-437.</ref> He is known especially for the [[Robin boundary condition]]. The [[French Academy of Sciences]] awarded him the ''Prix Francœur'' for 1893 and again for 1897 and the [[Poncelet Prize|''Prix Poncelet'']] for 1895.<ref>{{cite book|chapter=Science Prizes|title=The American Naturalist|year=1894|page=290|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nnEWAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA290}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|chapter=Tableau des prix décernés. Année 1897|title=Comptes rendus hebdomadaires des séances de l'Académie des sciences, Janvier – Juin 1898|year=1898|volume=Tome 126|page=165|location=Paris|publisher=Gauthier-Villars|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ymhAdwD_jxoC&pg=PA165}}</ref>
